90° is the angle between ligands on adjacent corners of an octahedron, the cis arrangement. Trans ligands sit on opposite sides of the metal.

Mixture II has Q = 3.0×10⁻⁵, below the K<sub>sp</sub> line at 4.9×10⁻⁵. When Q < K<sub>sp</sub>, the solution is unsaturated and more solid could still dissolve, so nothing precipitates.
Mixture I has Q = 1.2×10⁻⁵, well below the K<sub>sp</sub> line at 4.9×10⁻⁵. When Q < K<sub>sp</sub>, the solution is unsaturated, so no precipitate forms.
In I the two Cl ligands sit on adjacent corners, 90° apart, which makes it the cis isomer (cisplatin). Trans means the two Cl ligands are directly across the Pt, 180° apart.
III has two Br ligands, not two Cl, so it is Pt(NH₃)₂Br₂. Dichloro requires two chloride ligands, so its formula doesn't match the name.
IV has two Br ligands, not two Cl, so it is Pt(NH₃)₂Br₂. Dichloro requires two chloride ligands, so its formula doesn't match the name.
Cr³⁺ is d³, so it has only three d electrons. The diagram shows five electrons, one in each d orbital, so the metal ion must be d⁵.
Co³⁺ is d⁶, one more electron than the five drawn. NH₃ is fairly strong-field, so it would also pair all six in t₂g rather than spread them out singly.
This is ΔH° by itself. ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, and ΔS° is positive (a gas forms), so subtracting TΔS° makes ΔG° smaller than ΔH°.
A catalyst leaves K unchanged, but temperature does change K. For an endothermic reaction, heat acts like a reactant, so warming shifts the equilibrium and its constant.
I₂ is a reactant: it is used up in step 1 and still appears in the overall equation. An intermediate is made in one step and consumed in a later one, so it cancels out.
H₂ is a reactant: it is used up in step 2 and appears in the overall equation. An intermediate is made in an earlier step and consumed later, so it cancels out.
HI is the final product: it is made in step 2 and never used up, so it stays in the overall equation. An intermediate is made and then consumed, so it cancels out.
T sits in the exponent, −E<sub>a</sub>/RT, so changing T changes how negative the exponent is and therefore changes k. Only a zero E<sub>a</sub> would make k temperature-independent.
This is 0.400/(0.200 × 0.200), reactants over products. K<sub>c</sub> puts the products PCl₃ and Cl₂ on top and PCl₅ on the bottom.
H₂PO₄⁻ and HCO₃⁻ are the proton donors: H₂PO₄⁻ gives H⁺ in the forward reaction and HCO₃⁻ in the reverse. Bases are the species that accept those protons.
NO₂⁻ has no proton to give here; it is the conjugate base formed when HNO₂ donates H⁺. The strongest acid must be one of the two proton donors.
CH₃COO⁻ accepts a proton here, so it is a base, not an acid. The strongest acid must be one of the two species that donate H⁺.
AlCl₄⁻ is the adduct, the product formed after the acid–base bond is made. The Lewis acid is a reactant that accepts an electron pair.
AlCl₃ does not ionize here; Cl⁻ bonds directly to the Al atom of the intact molecule. That Al, with only six valence electrons and an empty orbital, accepts the lone pair.

76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is reasonable for a liquid metal: higher than typical solids, far below gases. The wrong entry is one that breaks the solid < liquid < gas order.
72 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is reasonable for an ionic solid like NaCl, well below any gas. The wrong entry is one that breaks the solid < liquid < gas order.
186 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is typical of a small gas molecule, since gases have the highest entropies. The wrong entry is one that breaks the solid < liquid < gas order.
+52.4 kJ is ΔH° − ΔG° at 298 K, which is TΔS° at 298 K. You still need ΔS° from it, then ΔG° = ΔH° − (800 K)ΔS°.
From ΔG° = −RT ln K, HF's larger K<sub>a</sub> gives the smaller ΔG° (+18.1 vs +42.9 kJ mol⁻¹). The acid with the less favorable ionization has the more positive ΔG°.
Both parts are reversed. Since ΔG° = −RT ln K<sub>a</sub>, the acid with the smaller K<sub>a</sub> has the more positive ΔG°, and the one with the larger K<sub>a</sub> is stronger.
ΔG°<sub>f</sub> of an element in its standard state, like H₂ or O₂, is zero by definition. So the table already gives everything needed to find ΔG° and K for both reactions.
K = e<sup>−ΔG°/RT</sup> is always positive, never zero. A zero K would mean no product at all, which is not an equilibrium mixture of A and B.
H⁺ is a reactant in solution, so it appears in Q, squared: Q = [Zn²⁺]P<sub>H₂</sub>/[H⁺]². Adding NaOH changes [H⁺], so it changes Q and the cell potential.
A neutron has Z = 0, but the charge balance needs a particle with Z = 1 (7 + 2 − 8). It does have A = 1, so only the mass balance works.
An electron has A = 0 and Z = −1, but the balances need A = 1 (14 + 4 − 17) and Z = 1 (7 + 2 − 8). Neither number matches.
A positron has the right charge (Z = 1) but A = 0. The mass balance, 14 + 4 − 17, needs a particle with A = 1.
A proton has A = 1, but the mass numbers already balance (13 = 13), so the emitted particle must have A = 0.
A neutron has A = 1 and Z = 0, but the mass numbers already balance (13 = 13) and Z drops from 7 to 6. The particle must carry A = 0 and Z = +1.
Curve X is acetone: it has the higher vapor pressure because its weaker intermolecular forces (no hydrogen bonding) let molecules escape more easily. X reaches 760 torr near 56 °C, not 100 °C.
